answer.label: Not Thomas Edison — an anonymous saying
answer.authorDates: Earliest printed May 1921 · author never identified
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Thomas Edison ever said or wrote this. According to Quote Investigator, the saying first appeared — uncredited — in a May 1921 Indiana newspaper, and Edison was not linked to it until 1962, thirty-one years after his death. The safest label for its origin is simply “anonymous.”

source.excerpt: The reason most people do not recognize an opportunity when they meet it is because it usually goes around wearing overalls and looking like Hard Work.
trail: The fullest chronology is Quote Investigator’s 2012 study, which finds the earliest instance in a May 1921 Indiana newspaper with no attribution.
QI notes the saying was later pinned on several different people — Henry Dodd (1922), Paul Larmer (1941) and Lila Kroppmann (1943) — before the Edison label surfaced in 1962.
Wikiquote lists the line only against a 1990 secondary book (John L. Mason’s An Enemy Called Average), with no Edison-era source.
source.excerptNote: The earliest documented form, printed anonymously in May 1921. The now-familiar wording (“Opportunity is missed by most people…”) is a later crystallization of this floating adage — not a sentence traceable to any single named author.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the full origin trail

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording has no identifiable author: it is a later form of an anonymous adage first printed in 1921. Because no single authored work or edition can be tied to this sentence, no copyright status can honestly be asserted — the underlying 1921 newspaper phrasing is old, but the modern wording’s provenance is simply unknown.

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.kicker: Popularly credited — but not the source
author.heading: Who Edison was
author.bio: Thomas Alva Edison was the prolific American inventor behind the phonograph, the practical incandescent light bulb and the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park. He is famous for genuinely hard-work-flavored lines — most authentically “Genius is one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration” — which is precisely why unrelated work-ethic sayings, like this one, tend to gravitate to his name. He died in 1931, three decades before anyone connected him to the “overalls” adage.

misattribution.heading: How Edison got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet” misattribution: a punchy, work-ethic adage of anonymous origin that drifted onto a famous hard-work icon decades after he died.

items.why: No Edison speech, letter, interview or notebook contains this line. Quote Investigator finds the first Edison credit only in 1962 — 31 years after his 1931 death — and rates the evidence “very weak.”

items.who: Henry Dodd, Paul Larmer, Lila Kroppmann
items.why: Before Edison, the same saying was credited to each of these figures in the 1920s–40s, none with real substantiation — a sign it was free-floating and authorless.
The oldest known printing — Indiana, May 1921 — carries no byline or attribution at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: this is an anonymous American adage from around 1921, not a Thomas Edison quotation.

context.heading: Why the line sticks to Edison
lead: The saying works because it flatters a specific worldview: that success is ordinary effort in disguise. Edison — the self-styled apostle of perspiration — is the perfect mascot for that idea, so the adage found a comfortable home under his name even though the paper trail points elsewhere.
What the record actually shows is a floating maxim that changed owners every few years until a famous name made it stop moving.
context.pull: An anonymous 1921 adage, not an Edison quotation.
